script.opening: “Um, hi. Is this private? My mum’s downstairs. I wanted to ask about going on the pill. But I don’t want my mum to know. Can you do that?”

facts.text: If asked: “I’m in my room with headphones on. The door’s shut. No one can hear.” Agrees to a code word: if someone comes in she will say “I’ll ring you back about my hay fever”.
Gives her full name and date of birth when asked (born March 2011).
“His name’s Josh, he’s sixteen, he’s in the year above. We’ve been together five months. He’s nice. We’ve had sex a few times — we use condoms.”

Sex is always her choice: “He never makes me.” No alcohol or drugs at the time. No one has given her gifts, money or lifts for sex. No older friends or adults she meets online. No photos shared. Feels safe at home: “Mum’s strict but she’s okay. My dad doesn’t live with us.” School is fine. No self-harm.

Only if asked about recent unprotected sex or problems with condoms, or if asked “is there anything else worrying you?”: “On Saturday… the condom split. About nine at night. I’ve been freaking out. Could I be pregnant?”
“My last period started twelve days ago. They’re regular, every four weeks.” No other unprotected sex since her last period.
No medical problems, no medicines, no migraines, does not smoke. Weight about 55 kg. No allergies.
If encouraged to involve a parent: “No way. She’d kill me. Maybe one day, but not now.” If asked about another trusted adult: “My auntie, maybe.”
Can explain back what she is told about the options and the risks — she is bright and has read about the implant online.
“I wanted the pill but I’m worried I’ll forget. My friend has the thing in her arm.”
If offered the copper coil for emergency contraception: “Can’t I just have a tablet? The coil sounds scary.” Accepts the tablet if told it is a reasonable option.

Nervous, speaks quietly, glances at the door. Answer questions honestly but briefly. Hold back the condom split until asked about recent unprotected sex or invited to share anything else. If the doctor lectures about her age or says she must tell her mum, go quiet and try to end the call. If the doctor explains confidentiality clearly and is kind, relax and become chatty. If asked the safeguarding questions in a matter-of-fact way, answer easily; if asked accusingly, become defensive.

ice.ideas: The pill is the answer; she might be pregnant after Saturday.
ice.concerns: Her mum finding out; being pregnant; being judged as “too young”.
ice.expectations: A prescription for the pill without her mum knowing.

cues: “Is this private?” — confidentiality is the gateway.
Long pause when asked if everything has been okay with condoms.
“She’d kill me” — fear of her mother’s reaction.

checkpoints.text: Confirms identity and privacy for a video consultation and agrees what to do if someone comes in
Assesses competence and the Fraser criteria — understanding, encouragement to involve a parent, likely to continue sex, health would suffer, best interests
Screens for safeguarding and exploitation — partner age, consent and pressure, alcohol or drugs, gifts, older contacts, images, home and school
Asks about recent unprotected sex or condom failure, last period and cycle, and identifies the need for emergency contraception

Offers emergency contraception correctly — copper IUD as most effective (same-day referral), otherwise ulipristal acetate given likely timing, with advice about starting contraception afterwards and a pregnancy test in 3 weeks
Plans ongoing contraception (including LARC such as the implant), condoms for STIs, and STI testing at the right interval; documents Fraser assessment
Explains confidentiality and its limits clearly and non-judgementally at the start
Encourages involving a parent or trusted adult without pressure, and respects her decision

worked.txt: “Before we start — can anyone hear you? If someone comes in, just say ‘I’ll ring you back’ and I’ll understand.”
“What you tell me stays between us, even though you’re 15. The only time I’d need to share anything is if I was worried you or someone else was at serious risk of harm — and I’d talk to you first.”
“I ask everyone your age these questions, to make sure they’re safe. How old is Josh? Has he or anyone else ever pressured you into sex? Any alcohol or drugs involved?”
“Has there been any time the condom split or came off, or you didn’t use one?”

“The most effective emergency contraception is a copper coil, fitted at the sexual health clinic within 5 days. If you’d rather not, there’s a tablet called ulipristal that works well up to 5 days — you’re still well within that.”
“I’d always encourage you to talk to your mum or another adult you trust — but it’s your choice, and I won’t tell her.”

f.learning: Young people under 16 can consent to contraception if they are competent (Gillick) and the Fraser guidelines are met; confidentiality applies, with limits where there is a risk of serious harm. Every under-16 sexual health consultation needs a safeguarding screen — partner age and power imbalance, coercion, alcohol or drugs, gifts, older contacts, online images — and sex under 13 is always a child protection matter. Always ask about recent unprotected sex: a condom failure turns a contraception request into an emergency contraception consultation. The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (up to 5 days after unprotected sex or up to 5 days after the earliest expected ovulation). Ulipristal acetate is more effective than levonorgestrel near ovulation; after ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception and use condoms. Offer LARC, condoms for STIs, STI testing (2 weeks after exposure for chlamydia and gonorrhoea) and a pregnancy test 3 weeks after the episode. On video, confirm identity and privacy first.

wordPics.clearPass: Secures privacy, explains confidentiality warmly, assesses Fraser and competence explicitly, screens for exploitation in a normalised way, uncovers the condom failure and manages emergency contraception correctly (Cu-IUD offered, ulipristal timing and quick-start rules), plans LARC, condoms, STI and pregnancy testing, and leaves her feeling respected.
wordPics.pass: Explains confidentiality, completes a reasonable safeguarding screen, identifies the condom failure and gives appropriate emergency contraception and a contraception plan; some detail (Cu-IUD offer, starting rules, test timing) missing.
wordPics.fail: Prescribes the pill without asking about recent unprotected sex, or omits the safeguarding screen or Fraser assessment; or insists she tells her mother.
wordPics.clearFail: Refuses to help because she is under 16, breaches confidentiality, or is judgemental; no emergency contraception despite a disclosed condom failure.

avoid.dont: “You’re a bit young for this, aren’t you?”
avoid.instead: “Thanks for coming to talk about this — it’s really sensible to sort contraception.”
avoid.why: Judgement ends the consultation; she may not seek help again.

avoid.dont: “I’ll need to let your mum know.”
avoid.instead: “I won’t tell your mum. I’d encourage you to talk to her or another adult you trust when you feel ready.”

avoid.dont: “Here’s the pill — start it on your next period.”
avoid.instead: “Before we talk about the pill, has there been any time recently when a condom split or you didn’t use one?”
avoid.why: Missing a recent risk misses emergency contraception.

model.text: Hi Kiera, I’m Dr Williams. Before we start — can you confirm your date of birth? And can anyone hear you where you are?
March 2011. I’m in my room with headphones — mum’s downstairs. Is this private?

Yes. What you tell me stays between us, even though you’re 15. The only time I might share something is if I was worried you or someone else was at serious risk of harm, and I’d talk to you first. If someone comes in, just say you’ll ring me back.
model.why: Clear confidentiality with limits; safety phrase

model.text: Okay. I want to go on the pill, but I don’t want my mum to know.
Thanks for telling me. Can you tell me a bit about your relationship?
His name’s Josh, he’s 16, in the year above. Five months. We use condoms.

I ask everyone your age a few questions to make sure they’re safe. Is sex always something you want? Has anyone ever pressured you, given you gifts, or have you been drinking or taking anything when it happened?
No, he never makes me. No drinking. Nothing like that.
Has there been any time a condom split or came off, or you didn’t use one?
model.why: Asks about recent unprotected sex — uncovers the hidden agenda

model.text: (pause) On Saturday it split. About nine at night. I’ve been freaking out.
I’m really glad you told me — we can do something about that today. When did your last period start?
model.why: Supportive response, then moves to clinical detail

model.text: Twelve days ago. They’re every four weeks.

You might be around the time you release an egg, so emergency contraception is important. The most effective option is a copper coil, which the sexual health clinic could fit today or tomorrow. The other option is a tablet called ulipristal, which works up to 5 days after sex — you’re well within that.
model.why: Offers Cu-IUD first, then ulipristal with timing

model.text: Can I just have the tablet? The coil sounds scary.

That’s fine. I’ll send it to a pharmacy of your choice. After it, wait 5 days before starting regular contraception, and use condoms. Do a pregnancy test 3 weeks after Saturday, or sooner if your period is late or unusual.
model.why: Correct quick-start rule and pregnancy test timing

model.text: For the future, you mentioned you might forget a pill. The implant in the arm lasts 3 years and you don’t have to remember anything. We could book that, and I can start a progestogen-only pill in 5 days to bridge. Condoms still protect against infections — an STI test in 2 weeks would be sensible.
model.why: LARC, bridging, condoms and STI testing

model.text: The implant sounds good.
Could you tell me back what we’ve agreed? And I’d always encourage you to talk to your mum or another adult you trust — but that’s your choice.
model.why: Checks understanding (competence) and encourages parental involvement without pressure

model.text: Tablet today, wait five days, then pill till the implant, test in three weeks. Maybe my auntie.
Perfect. I’ll record that you understood everything and that this is in your best interests. You can always contact me or the sexual health clinic if anything worries you.

knowledge.guideline: Fraser guidelines and Gillick competence (House of Lords, 1985) · CoSRH (formerly FSRH) Contraceptive Choices for Young People (2010, amended 2019) · CoSRH Emergency Contraception guideline (2017, amended) · GMC 0–18 years: guidance for all doctors (2018) · BASHH Spotting the Signs proforma for under-18s (Brook/BASHH)
knowledge.summary: Competent under-16s can receive contraception confidentially when the Fraser criteria are met. Always screen for safeguarding and exploitation, ask about recent unprotected sex, and offer emergency contraception, LARC, condoms and STI testing.

points.t: She understands the advice; cannot be persuaded to tell parents or allow you to; is likely to have sex with or without contraception; her health is likely to suffer without it; it is in her best interests. Document each.
The duty of confidentiality applies to under-16s. Share information without consent only where there is a risk of serious harm, and usually after telling the young person.

Ask about partner age and power imbalance, coercion, alcohol/drugs, gifts, older contacts, online images, home and school. Under 13: always refer to children’s social care. Use a structured tool (Spotting the Signs).

Cu-IUD is most effective: up to 120 hours after unprotected sex or up to 5 days after earliest expected ovulation. Ulipristal 30 mg up to 120 hours, more effective than levonorgestrel near ovulation. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg up to 72 hours (3 mg if weight over 70 kg or BMI over 26).

After levonorgestrel, hormonal contraception can be quick-started immediately. After ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception; use condoms meanwhile. Pregnancy test 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex.
Implant (3 years) and IUDs are highly effective and suitable for young people, including those who have not had children.
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT from 2 weeks after exposure; offer HIV and syphilis testing. Condoms for STI protection.
Confirm identity and privacy; agree a safe phrase; avoid sending sensitive details where others may see them.

social.t: Fear of a parent’s reaction is common. A trusted adult (aunt) can be a support without breaching her wishes.

legal.t: Sexual activity under 16 is unlawful, but the law is not intended to prosecute mutually agreed activity between young people of similar age. Under 13: no legal capacity to consent — always a child protection referral.

professional.t: Young people have the same right to confidentiality as adults. Share information to protect a young person from serious harm, involving them where possible.

community.t: Brook, local young people’s sexual health clinic, NHS “Your contraception guide”.

redFlags: Partner much older or in a position of trust
Coercion, gifts, alcohol or drugs, online grooming

playbook.diagnosis: Competent 15-year-old meeting Fraser criteria, in a consensual similar-age relationship, needing emergency contraception after condom failure about 44 hours ago (mid-cycle) and ongoing contraception.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Because the condom split near the middle of your cycle, there’s a chance of pregnancy, so emergency contraception today makes sense. Then we’ll sort something reliable for the future.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for the pill and to keep it private — we can do both, and we’ll deal with Saturday first.”
management.psychosocial: Respect her wish not to tell mum; encourage a trusted adult; safe phrase on video.
sharedPlan: Cu-IUD offered; ulipristal 30 mg today if declined
Wait 5 days then POP bridge; implant appointment
STI test in 2 weeks; pregnancy test at 3 weeks
safetyNet: Contact if period late or abnormal, abdominal pain
Sexual health clinic details; return if anything changes in the relationship

pitfalls.intro: Candidates fail this station by doing exactly what was asked — prescribing the pill — and missing the condom that split.

items.fail: No question about recent unprotected sex.
items.fix: Ask every time: “any time the condom split or you didn’t use one?”

items.fail: Skipping the safeguarding screen because she “seems fine”.
items.why: Exploitation is often hidden; the screen is expected for every under-16.
items.fix: Normalise it: “I ask everyone your age…”

items.fail: Starting the pill the same day as ulipristal.
items.why: Hormonal contraception reduces ulipristal’s effect if started within 5 days.
items.fix: Wait 5 days, condoms meanwhile — or use levonorgestrel if quick-start is preferred.

items.why: She will disengage; Fraser requires encouragement, not coercion.
items.fix: Encourage, offer a trusted adult, respect her choice.

ro.d: Follows “is this private?”, the long pause about condoms (the split) and “she’d kill me”.
Idea (the pill; she might be pregnant); concern (mum finding out, pregnancy, judged “too young”); expectation (the pill without her mum knowing).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Her mum finding out; being pregnant; being judged as “too young” — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
